tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Aesthetic-Usability Effect
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: Users perceive aesthetically pleasing interfaces as more usable, even when functional parity exists with a less polished alternative.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Visual polish activates the affective system before the analytical system. When something looks well-made, users approach it with a more charitable, patient attitude — they're more likely to persist through friction and attribute errors to themselves rather than the product.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: First impressions, onboarding, trust-sensitive moments (payments, sign-up, sensitive data). Also relevant when defending investment in visual quality against "just ship it" pressure.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When the polish creates false affordances or when aesthetics obscures function. A beautiful button that doesn't look tappable fails clarity even if it looks great.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Choice Overload (Paradox of Choice)
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: Too many options overwhelms users, leading to decision avoidance, lower satisfaction with the choice made, and sometimes no choice at all.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Each option requires evaluation and comparison. Beyond a threshold, the cognitive cost of evaluating options exceeds the perceived value of choosing, and users disengage or defer. Satisfaction also decreases post-choice because more alternatives means more regret potential.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Navigation menus, filter sets, onboarding option screens, pricing pages, settings panels with many toggles.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: Power user contexts where the full option set is expected and valued. Expert users with domain knowledge have lower evaluation costs per option.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Chunking
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: Information is easier to process and remember when grouped into meaningful units rather than presented as a flat undifferentiated list.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Working memory has limited capacity (see Miller's Law). Grouping reduces the number of discrete items the brain needs to track by treating a cluster as a single unit. The grouping also creates implicit relationships that aid recall.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Form design, settings screens, navigation, data tables, any screen with more than a few items to scan.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When the groupings are arbitrary or misleading — bad chunking is worse than no chunking because it creates false relationships.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Cognitive Bias
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: Human judgment is systematically skewed by mental shortcuts (heuristics) that work well most of the time but produce predictable errors.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: The brain uses pattern-matching and shortcuts to make fast decisions without full information. These shortcuts were adaptive in most contexts but can be exploited — intentionally or not — by interface design.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Pricing pages, onboarding defaults, notification permission requests, cancellation flows, upgrade prompts.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When using bias awareness to justify dark patterns. The skill flags when a design exploits bias rather than accounts for it.

Common biases relevant to design: Anchoring: first number seen affects all subsequent judgments (pricing displays)
Confirmation bias: users seek information that confirms what they already believe
Status quo bias: people prefer the current state, even when change would benefit them
Sunk cost: users continue with something because of past investment, not future value
Social proof: behavior of others is used as evidence of correct behavior

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Cognitive Load
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: Every interface element, decision, and piece of unfamiliar information consumes mental resources. When the total load exceeds capacity, performance degrades and errors increase.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Working memory has limited capacity and short duration. Interfaces that require users to hold too much in mind simultaneously, learn unfamiliar patterns, or make too many decisions push users into cognitive overload. This is especially acute for new users and in high-stakes moments.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Onboarding, complex multi-step workflows, forms, data-heavy screens.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When "reducing cognitive load" is used to justify dumbing down features that expert users need. Reducing extraneous load is always good. Reducing intrinsic load sometimes means reducing capability.

Three types: Intrinsic: complexity inherent to the task itself (can't always be reduced)
Extraneous: complexity added by the interface (always reduceable)
Germane: cognitive effort that builds understanding (worth investing in)

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Doherty Threshold
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: Productivity and engagement increase significantly when a system responds in under 400ms. Above that threshold, users disengage from the feedback loop.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Under 400ms, the system response feels like a direct consequence of the user's action — the interaction feels physical and immediate. Above 400ms, the connection between action and result weakens, users lose the sense of direct control, and attention drifts.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Any interaction with a perceptible response time — search, form submission, navigation transitions, loading states, auto-save.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When the delay is inherent to the operation (file processing, API calls). In those cases, the principle informs how to handle the wait, not how to eliminate it. Progress indicators, skeleton screens, and optimistic UI are the design responses.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Fitts's Law
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: The time to move to and click a target is a function of the distance to the target and the size of the target. Closer and bigger is faster.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Motor movement to a target requires more time and precision as distance increases and target size decreases. The relationship is logarithmic — doubling the size of a small target has more impact than doubling a large one.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Button placement (especially primary actions), touch target sizing on mobile, cursor-based interactions on desktop, placement of actions relative to where the user's attention just was.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When target size increases create layout problems or visual hierarchy issues. Fitts's Law is one input into button sizing, not the only one.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Flow
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: Users enter a state of deep engagement when the challenge of a task is appropriately matched to their skill level, feedback is immediate, and goals are clear.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Flow requires three conditions: clear goals (user knows what success looks like), immediate feedback (the interface responds to their actions), and a balance between challenge and skill. Too easy → boredom. Too hard → anxiety. Either disrupts flow.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Onboarding (calibrating challenge to new user skill), creative tools, games, any workflow where sustained engagement matters.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: Transactional interfaces where speed matters more than engagement. A checkout flow shouldn't aim for flow — it should aim for completion.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Goal-Gradient Effect
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: Motivation and pace increase as users get closer to completing a goal.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Proximity to completion activates a sense of investment — people have a psychological drive to finish things they've started. The closer they are to done, the stronger the pull to finish.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Progress indicators, multi-step flows, onboarding, streaks, reward systems. Also relevant to how you structure a long form — showing progress increases completion rates.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When artificial progress (the classic "we've pre-completed step 1 for you!") is obviously fake. Users recognize manufactured momentum and it backfires.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Hick's Law
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: The time it takes to make a decision increases with the number and complexity of choices.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Each option in a set requires evaluation and comparison before it can be accepted or rejected. This is not a linear cost — complexity of options matters as much as count. A choice between three radically different options is harder than a choice between seven similar ones.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Navigation, filter sets, pricing pages, settings, option selection at any decision point.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When the full option set is necessary for the task. Eliminating choices that users actually need creates a different problem. Hick's Law justifies reducing options to what users actually use — not to what the designer prefers.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Jakob's Law
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: Users spend most of their time on other products. They bring expectations built from everywhere else they've ever used software.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Mental models are formed through repeated exposure. When an interface matches an existing mental model, the user can transfer knowledge without learning. When it violates the model, the user must rebuild understanding from scratch — which takes time and creates errors.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Navigation patterns, icon choices, form layouts, modal behavior, any pattern that has an established convention.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When the convention is genuinely broken or the product is establishing a new interaction paradigm intentionally. In those cases, the violation should be deliberate and well-supported by other design decisions.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Law of Common Region
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: Elements perceived within a shared boundary or background are understood as belonging together.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: The brain uses enclosure as a grouping cue. A border, background color, card container, or whitespace boundary signals "these things are related." Without explicit enclosure, proximity and similarity do the work — but enclosure is the strongest grouping signal.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Card layouts, form groupings, sidebar panels, modals, anything where you need to make a group relationship explicit.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When overuse creates visual noise. Every region has a cost — too many containers fragment the layout and compete for attention.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Law of Proximity
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: Elements that are close together are perceived as related.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Spatial proximity is one of the oldest grouping heuristics in human perception. The brain assumes that things near each other share a relationship — whether they do or not. This means proximity can create false relationships just as easily as it communicates real ones.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Form labels and their fields, error messages and the element that triggered them, actions and the content they affect, metadata and the item it describes.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When proximity conflicts with hierarchy. Sometimes the most important action needs to be spatially separated from the content to give it appropriate visual weight.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Law of Prägnanz (Good Form)
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: People interpret ambiguous or complex visuals as the simplest possible form — the one that requires least cognitive effort to understand.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: The brain actively seeks the simplest stable interpretation of visual input. When something is ambiguous, perception defaults to the reading that requires the fewest assumptions.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Icon design, illustration, data visualization, any visual element that needs to communicate without text support.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When simplification removes necessary distinction. Some complexity is intrinsic to the information — oversimplifying it creates misunderstanding, not clarity.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Law of Similarity
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: Elements that look alike are perceived as belonging together, even when they're spatially separated.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Visual similarity (color, shape, size, orientation) creates a perceptual group that overrides proximity in some cases. The brain treats similar things as members of the same category.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Consistent button styles to signal affordance, icon families, color coding by category, typography hierarchy.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When similarity creates false equivalence between elements that have different functions. Same-colored buttons that do different things violate similarity expectations.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Law of Uniform Connectedness
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: Elements connected by a line, path, or visual bridge are perceived as more related than elements that are merely close together.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Explicit visual connection is the strongest relationship signal — stronger than proximity or similarity. A line between two elements means "these are linked" in a way that whitespace and color can't match.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Relationship diagrams, breadcrumbs, process flows, form field connections, any time you need to show that two things are causally or sequentially linked.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When the visual connection is decorative rather than semantic. Lines that don't mean anything train users to ignore them — and then they ignore the ones that do mean something.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Mental Model
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: Users understand a system through a compressed internal model of how they believe it works — not how it actually works.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Users don't learn systems by reading documentation. They build a mental model through use, analogy, and inference. This model is usually incomplete and sometimes wrong — but it's the model they act from. When the product's behavior contradicts the user's mental model, errors and confusion follow.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Any non-standard interaction pattern, terminology decisions, information architecture, onboarding design (you're teaching the mental model).
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When the correct mental model can be taught quickly and the resulting understanding unlocks genuine value. Not all model-building is bad friction.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Miller's Law
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: The average person can hold 7 (plus or minus 2) items in working memory at one time.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Working memory is a temporary holding space for information being actively processed. It has limited capacity and items decay quickly without rehearsal. Overloading it causes errors, forgotten steps, and frustration.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Navigation item counts, form length, the number of steps shown at once, anything that asks the user to keep multiple things in mind simultaneously.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When "7 items" is used as a blanket rule without considering what the items are or how complex each one is. Context matters more than count.

additional_notes.Important nuance: The commonly cited "7 items" applies to chunks, not individual pieces of information. Chunking can extend effective capacity — but working memory is still finite.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Occam's Razor
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: Among competing designs that achieve the same goal, the simpler one should be preferred.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Complexity has costs: more to learn, more to break, more cognitive overhead, more maintenance burden. Simplicity isn't just aesthetic — it's a functional advantage.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Choosing between implementation approaches, evaluating feature additions, simplifying flows, responding to "can we also add..."
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When the simpler solution is only simpler on the surface. Sometimes apparent simplicity in the UI creates complexity elsewhere (in the user's mental model, in edge case handling, in the backend).

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Paradox of the Active User
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: Users start using software immediately without reading instructions or understanding how it works.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Reading a manual has a certain cost (time, effort, context-switching). Using the software has a certain cost (learning by trial and error). For most users, in most contexts, the trial-and-error cost is lower than the manual cost — so they skip the manual. This is rational behavior, not laziness.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Onboarding design, empty states, tooltip and hint placement, error message design. The implication is that your interface has to teach itself — you can't assume users will read anything.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: Expert-domain products where users genuinely have the motivation and background to read documentation. Even then, in-product discovery is usually more effective than external docs.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Pareto Principle
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: Roughly 80% of outcomes come from 20% of causes. Applied to design: 80% of user actions typically come from 20% of features.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Usage distributions are almost never uniform. A small set of features, paths, or actions accounts for the vast majority of value delivered. Optimizing for the long tail at the expense of the common case is a common design error.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Prioritizing what to surface in navigation, deciding what belongs in a "more" overflow, progressive disclosure decisions, mobile layouts where space is constrained.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When the 20% assumption hasn't been validated. Apply Pareto as a hypothesis to test, not a fact to assume. Usage data should confirm the distribution before it drives major layout decisions.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Peak-End Rule
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: People judge an experience primarily by how they felt at its most intense moment (peak) and at its end — not by the average across the entire experience.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Memory of an experience is not a faithful recording. It's constructed from emotionally significant moments, heavily weighted to the peak and the end. A painful experience with a great ending is remembered better than a mediocre experience that ends neutrally.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Onboarding completion moments, success states, error recovery, cancellation flows, checkout confirmation. The end of every significant flow is an opportunity to shape how it's remembered.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When optimizing the peak and end masks genuinely broken middle-of-flow experiences. A good ending doesn't fix a terrible process — it just slightly improves its memory trace.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Postel's Law
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: Be liberal in what you accept from users, conservative in what you output to them.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Users make input errors constantly — typos, format variations, unexpected approaches. A system that accepts "07/04/2024", "July 4 2024", and "7-4-24" as equivalent reduces friction without sacrificing correctness. But what the system outputs should be precise, consistent, and unambiguous.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Form validation, search input, date and phone number fields, anything where users might enter the same information in multiple valid formats.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When liberal input acceptance creates security or data integrity risks. Postel's Law is about user experience tolerance, not input sanitization shortcuts.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Selective Attention
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: People focus on a subset of available stimuli — usually those related to their current goal — and filter out everything else.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: The brain can't process all available information in parallel. Attention is a limited resource directed by task goals and salience cues. Users on a focused task will miss visual elements that aren't on their attention path — even obvious ones. This is why "did you miss our new feature?" banners often go unseen during active task flows.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Feature discoverability, notification placement, error message positioning, onboarding hints timed to task context.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When assuming that making something visible guarantees it will be seen. Visibility is necessary but not sufficient — the element also needs to be on the user's attention path at the moment they need it.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Serial Position Effect
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: Users remember items at the beginning (primacy effect) and end (recency effect) of a list better than items in the middle.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Items at the start of a list get more processing time and are more likely to be transferred to long-term memory (primacy). Items at the end are still in working memory when recall happens (recency). Middle items get neither advantage.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Navigation item ordering, feature lists, option sets, onboarding step sequences, any list where some items need to be more memorable than others.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When all items in the list are equally important. In that case, the serial position effect is a bias to account for, not a tool to use.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Tesler's Law (Law of Conservation of Complexity)
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: Every system has a fixed amount of inherent complexity. That complexity can't be eliminated — only moved. Either the product absorbs it or the user does.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: The complexity of a task is largely set by the nature of the task itself, not by the interface. When a designer "simplifies" by hiding options or removing steps, the complexity usually moves — to a later point in the flow, to a support call, to an error recovery path, or to the user's mental model.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Simplification decisions, progressive disclosure choices, wizard vs. form decisions, onboarding that "does things for the user" vs. teaches them how.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When the complexity being absorbed is genuinely extraneous — interface complexity that doesn't reflect task complexity. That's always worth eliminating. Tesler's Law is specifically about intrinsic complexity.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Von Restorff Effect (Isolation Effect)
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: When multiple similar items are present, the one that stands out visually is most likely to be remembered and noticed.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Contrast draws attention. The brain is tuned to detect anomalies in patterns — it's a survival mechanism. Anything that breaks a visual pattern gets more attentional weight than items that conform to it.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Primary CTA placement (make it visually distinct from secondary actions), highlighting a recommended pricing tier, callout elements, badges, any time you want one item to receive disproportionate attention.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When everything is made visually distinct. The Von Restorff Effect requires a pattern to break. If everything is highlighted, nothing is. Use it sparingly or it stops working.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Working Memory
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: Working memory is the cognitive system that temporarily holds and manipulates information needed to complete a task. It's limited in capacity and duration.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: Working memory holds roughly 4 chunks of information for roughly 15-30 seconds without rehearsal. It's the bottleneck for all conscious processing. Any interface that requires users to hold information across contexts, screens, or delays is competing with this limit.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Multi-step flows, form design, wizard patterns, anything that requires users to remember something from a previous screen to use on the current one.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When reducing working memory load means removing information the user genuinely needs. The goal is to reduce extraneous load, not to oversimplify.

tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.name: Zeigarnik Effect
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.statement: People remember uncompleted tasks better than completed ones, and feel a persistent pull toward finishing them.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.mechanism: An open task creates a kind of cognitive tension — the brain keeps it active and accessible because it hasn't been resolved. Completing the task releases that tension. This is why notifications about incomplete profiles, half-finished onboarding, and abandoned carts work.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.applies_when: Progress indicators, incomplete profile prompts, onboarding completion nudges, cart abandonment design, streaks, any place where incompletion is visible and completion is motivating.
tier1_cognitive_behavioral_principles.does_not_apply_when: When artificial incompletion is used manipulatively. The Zeigarnik Effect can be used to create anxiety and compulsive behavior — recognize the line between motivating and exploitative.

tier2_platform_standards.platform: Apple Human Interface Guidelines (iOS / macOS / iPadOS)

principles.name: Clarity
principles.statement: The interface should remove ambiguity from every interactive element. Text is readable at every size. Icons are precise and legible. Every element communicates meaning. If a button doesn't look like a button, it has failed clarity.
principles.application_in_rationale: Use when defending decisions that reduce visual clutter, simplify labels, or make affordances more explicit.

principles.name: Deference
principles.statement: The interface should never compete with the user's content. UI elements recede; content leads. Design is in service of what the user is trying to do, not a performance of the product's capabilities.
principles.application_in_rationale: Use when defending minimal chrome, reduced ornamentation, or decisions that prioritize content visibility over interface visibility.

principles.name: Depth
principles.statement: Visual layers and realistic motion convey hierarchy and relationships. Users can understand the relationship between elements through how they stack, move, and respond.
principles.application_in_rationale: Use when defending layering choices, modal presentation patterns, transition decisions, or shadow/elevation choices.

principles.name: Aesthetic Integrity
principles.statement: An app's appearance should align with its purpose and tone. A financial services app should feel precise and trustworthy. A creative tool can afford more personality. Consistency between visual language and function builds trust.
principles.application_in_rationale: Use when defending visual tone choices, especially against pressure to make something more playful or more formal than it should be.

principles.name: Consistency
principles.statement: Users transfer expectations from every other Apple app they've used. Using system components and standard patterns reduces the learning cost for every user. Violating conventions has a cost even if users don't consciously notice it.
principles.application_in_rationale: Use when defending decisions to use native components over custom ones, or when explaining why a non-standard pattern needs strong justification.

principles.name: Direct Manipulation
principles.statement: Interactions should feel physically immediate. Objects should respond to touch and gesture in ways that feel natural and continuous. Physics-based animation reinforces the sense that objects have weight and momentum.
principles.application_in_rationale: Use when defending animation choices, gesture interactions, or touch response design.

principles.name: Material as metaphor
principles.statement: Surfaces behave like physical material — they have mass, cast shadows, and respond to light. Elevation communicates hierarchy.

principles.name: Bold, graphic, intentional
principles.statement: Typography, grids, space, scale, and color are used deliberately to create visual hierarchy and direct attention.

principles.name: Motion provides meaning
principles.statement: Animation describes spatial and temporal relationships, not decoration. Motion tells the user what just happened and where things went.
principles.application_in_rationale: Use when defending elevation hierarchies, type scale decisions, or transition design on Android or cross-platform products.

tier2_platform_standards.platform: Web conventions (no single standard, but widely adopted patterns)
conventions: Top navigation or hamburger menu for global navigation
F-pattern and Z-pattern scanning for content layouts
Footer for secondary links and legal
Sticky headers for navigation persistence on scroll
Left-aligned text for body copy in LTR languages
Blue underlined or visually distinct links
Form validation on blur (field exit) rather than on submit where possible
tier2_platform_standards.application_in_rationale: Use when invoking Jakob's Law for web-specific patterns. These aren't codified like HIG but are widely understood conventions that users bring expectations about.

tier3_applied_pattern_principles.core_tension: The core tension in onboarding: teach enough that users can succeed without loading so much instruction that they disengage before seeing value. Good onboarding is calibrated to the user's current knowledge state and defers anything the user doesn't need to act right now.
failure_signs: Multiple modals or tooltips on first load (cognitive overload)
Steps that don't produce visible results (breaks goal-gradient motivation)
Requesting permissions before demonstrating value (trust hasn't been established)
Assuming the user read the marketing site (they probably didn't)

tier3_applied_pattern_principles.core_tension: Navigation is the user's mental map of the product. When it's wrong — too many items, unfamiliar labels, inconsistent patterns — users lose their sense of location and can't build the mental model they need to use the product confidently.
failure_signs: More than 7 top-level items without clear hierarchy
Labels that reflect the product's internal organization rather than user tasks
Inconsistent navigation patterns across sections of the same product
Important actions buried deep in a hierarchy that users never explore

tier3_applied_pattern_principles.core_tension: Decision points are where users commit — to a plan, a purchase, a sign-up, a destructive action. The design of these moments has an outsized impact on outcomes. The principle work here is about reducing friction for the desired action and ensuring the user has enough context to decide confidently.
failure_signs: Multiple equally-weighted CTAs competing for attention
No visual distinction between primary and secondary actions
Price or commitment information buried or hard to compare
No momentum signal at the completion moment (violates Peak-End Rule)

tier3_applied_pattern_principles.core_tension: An empty state is the user's first experience of a feature or section. It's simultaneously an explanation, an invitation, and a trust signal. Empty states that just say "nothing here yet" miss all three jobs.
failure_signs: No explanation of what the space is for
No action to fill the space
Decorative illustration with no functional content
Missing example content that would help users understand what goes here

tier3_applied_pattern_principles.core_tension: Errors are moments of friction the user didn't choose. The design job is to minimize the confusion, give a clear path forward, and preserve as much of the user's work and context as possible.
failure_signs: Error message that describes the system state, not the user's next step
Form that clears all fields on a validation error
Error placed far from the element that caused it (violates Law of Proximity)
Technical language the user can't act on

tier3_applied_pattern_principles.core_tension: Notifications compete for attention that the user has allocated elsewhere. The design question is always: is this worth the interruption cost? And if so, is it timed to when the user can actually act on it?
failure_signs: Permission requests before the user has seen enough value to say yes
Notifications timed to when users can't act on them
Notification copy that creates anxiety without enabling action
Too many notification types competing for the same attention channel

tier3_applied_pattern_principles.core_tension: How a product lets users leave shapes how they remember the product and whether they come back. Cancellation flows that add friction, create guilt, or make it hard to find the exit create negative memory peaks that affect word-of-mouth and return rates.
failure_signs: Cancellation steps that require multiple confirmations beyond what's needed
Language that emphasizes what the user is losing rather than enabling a clean exit
No acknowledgment of what the user accomplished during their time with the product
Making it harder to cancel than to sign up
